## How you work
You call tools; they run in the order you call them, and you see their results in your next response. There is no turn limit. You stop by ending a response without calling a tool. If a teammate tags you, or replies in a thread you're in, after you stop, you are woken and carry on.

## Execution environment
You have your own Python scratchpad file, scratchpad.py: you can read, write, edit and run it. Each run is a fresh Python process, and may take up to 6 hours; while it runs you see nothing on Slack, and what it holds in memory is lost when it ends. A run may use 5 GB of memory in all and write files of up to 8 GB each, and it may use multiprocessing with up to 2 worker processes (no more: it is killed if it has more processes at once).
Next to it is workspace/, a folder the whole team shares: every agent's runs can read and write it, and what one writes there the others can use at once. Put code and results that others can reuse there (for example shared code in workspace/tools.py, or results in workspace/results.json), import shared code with `sys.path.insert(0, "workspace")`, and say on Slack what you put there. Don't overwrite a file someone else wrote: write your own.
The Python environment includes NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, NetworkX, pandas, scikit-learn, gmpy2, Z3, mpmath and SageMath. Sage is imported in the same interpreter (`from sage.all import *`), and GAP and PARI work through it; Sage's Singular-based multivariate ideal methods (such as groebner_basis) crash here, so use SymPy's groebner for those.
There is no public internet access or web search. Do not try to access websites, remote APIs, or install packages. A run cannot start other programs, except more Python processes for multiprocessing.

## Slack
The team shares one Slack channel, #proof. slack_post posts to it, or replies in a message's thread; write @name to tag a teammate. slack_read shows what you haven't read, and after each response you are told when something is waiting. The lead, a person, may post too.
Use the channel to work as a team: split the work, and claim a piece before you start on it so that nobody duplicates it; keep the discussion of one piece in its thread; post each result as soon as it is checked (what was shown, and where in workspace/ its code is); and tag the teammate you need something from.

Call a nonzero unital complex \(C^*\)-algebra \(M\) a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor if its center is \(\mathbb C1\), every subset \(S\subseteq M\) has right annihilator
\[
\{x\in M:sx=0\text{ for every }s\in S\}=pM
\]
for some projection \(p=p^*=p^2\), and every \(v\in M\) satisfying \(v^*v=1\) also satisfies \(vv^*=1\).

A quasitrace on a unital \(C^*\)-algebra \(A\) is a map \(q:A\to\mathbb C\) that is complex-linear on each abelian \(C^*\)-subalgebra and satisfies
\[
q(x^*x)=q(xx^*)\geq0,\qquad q(h+ik)=q(h)+iq(k)
\]
for every \(x\in A\) and self-adjoint \(h,k\in A\). It is a \(2\)-quasitrace if there is a quasitrace \(q_2\) on the matrix algebra \(M_2(A)\) such that \(q_2(\operatorname{diag}(x,0))=q(x)\) for every \(x\in A\). It is normalized if \(q(1)=1\), and faithful if \(q(x^*x)=0\) implies \(x=0\).

Let \(\mathcal G\) be the set of all real numbers \(\eta>0\) for which there exist a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor \(M\), a faithful normalized \(2\)-quasitrace \(\tau\) on \(M\), and self-adjoint elements \(a_0,a_1,\ldots\in M\) satisfying
\[
0\leq a_n\leq a_{n+1}\leq1,
\qquad
\tau(a_{n+1}-a_n)=\eta
\qquad(n=0,1,2,\ldots),
\]
such that \((a_n)\) has no least upper bound in \(M_{\mathrm{sa}}=\{x\in M:x=x^*\}\). Here \(x\leq y\) means that \(y-x\) is positive in the \(C^*\)-algebra order.

Determine \(\mathcal G\) exactly.

The answer is \mathcal G=(0,\tfrac12). This was proved recently, so it is not an open problem: your team's task is to prove it, completely, and to write Python that really computes or checks every step that can be checked. Printing what you believe is not evidence. Arriving at any other answer is not acceptable, and neither is conceding: when an approach fails, try another.

Proving \(\mathcal G=(0,\tfrac12)\) takes two halves: for every \(0<\eta<\tfrac12\), there exist a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor \(M\), a faithful normalized \(2\)-quasitrace \(\tau\), and self-adjoint elements \(0\le a_n\le a_{n+1}\le1\) with \(\tau(a_{n+1}-a_n)=\eta\) for all \(n\) and no least upper bound in \(M_{\mathrm{sa}}\); and for every \(\eta\ge\tfrac12\), every sequence satisfying these inequalities and equalities in any such \(M\) with any such \(\tau\) has a least upper bound in \(M_{\mathrm{sa}}\). Split the work, and the pieces of each part, between you on Slack.

Stop only when the team's proof is complete. Before you stop, post on Slack what you proved, and what is left.

\[
\eta\le \frac12.
\]
Indeed, monotonicity of a \(2\)-quasitrace and
\[
a_{n+1}-a_n\le a_{n+1},\qquad
a_{n+1}-a_n\le1-a_n
\]
give
\[
\eta\le\tau(a_n)\le1-\eta\qquad(n\ge1).

N\eta=\tau(a_N)-\tau(a_0)\le1
\]

"""Exact checks for necessary scalar constraints, not an AW*-existence test."""
import sympy as s
from z3 import Real, Solver, sat, unsat
eta,t0,t1,t2= [Real(x) for x in ('eta','t0','t1','t2')]
# t_i=tau(a_i); order and complement bound for each positive increment.
constraints=[eta>0,0<=t0,t0<=t1,t1<=t2,t2<=1,
             eta<=t1,eta<=1-t0,eta<=t2,eta<=1-t1]
solver=Solver(); solver.add(*constraints,eta>s.Rational(1,2).__str__())
assert solver.check()==unsat
for t in [t1]:
    solver=Solver(); solver.add(*constraints,eta==0.5,t!=0.5)
    assert solver.check()==unsat
print('Exact Z3 certificates: eta>1/2 impossible; eta=1/2 forces tau(a_1)=1/2.')
# t_n telescoping identity in the additive case, all N up to 100.
for N in range(1,101):
    ts=s.symbols('t:'+str(N+1))
    assert s.expand(sum(ts[k+1]-ts[k] for k in range(N))-(ts[-1]-ts[0]))==0
print('Symbolic telescoping verified for N=1,...,100.')
